title: The forgiveness chant
hook: a Theravada practice: if I've harmed anyone, I ask forgiveness; if anyone harmed me, I forgive (traditional)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Bharadvaja, and an insult the Buddha declined, left with the man who brought it. Your line was yours to keep.

A few short sentences, said slowly, pointing in different directions. If I have harmed anyone, in thought, word or deed, knowingly or unknowingly, I ask their forgiveness. If anyone has harmed me, knowingly or unknowingly, I forgive them. And in some versions, a further line, turned back toward the speaker: for the ways I have harmed myself, I forgive myself. Versions of it are taught in meditation halls today, with roots in Theravada Buddhist practice.
screen: `IF I HAVE HARMED ANYONE.` → `IF ANYONE HAS HARMED ME.` → `AND, IN SOME VERSIONS, MYSELF.`

segments.voice: Out, in, and back: asking forgiveness, giving it, and turning it toward yourself. The practice doesn't choose between them. It does them together, each time. That matters, because one is often easier than the others. Some people find asking easy and forgiving hard; for others it's the reverse. Saying them side by side keeps either from hiding. Then a small phrase that does a lot of work: knowingly or unknowingly. It admits that some of the harm we've done we'll never know about, and that some of the harm done to us was never meant. It forgives without waiting for a full account of who did what. The roots are older. In the Pali texts, owning a wrong and having it accepted is part of the path. In the Digha Nikaya, the Buddha tells a king who has confessed a terrible wrong that seeing a fault as a fault, making amends, and holding back in future is growth in the discipline of the noble ones. Monks in the Theravada tradition still ask one another's forgiveness, in set words, at certain times. And it's said slowly. It isn't meant to be said once and checked off. Some teachers, the meditation teacher Jack Kornfield among them, teach repeating it many times, over time, and noticing what resists: a face that won't come into focus, a line that sticks in the throat. That's not failure. It's the part of the work that's still to do.
screen: `ASK, FORGIVE, AND TURN IT BACK.` · `KNOWINGLY OR UNKNOWINGLY.` · `ROOTS IN THE PALI TEXTS.` · `SAID SLOWLY, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · then, large: `I ASK, I FORGIVE.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, say the lines slowly, silently or under your breath, with a few breaths between them: if I have harmed anyone, knowingly or unknowingly, I ask their forgiveness; if anyone has harmed me, knowingly or unknowingly, I forgive them, as far as I'm able today. If it feels right, add a last line toward yourself, and without forcing any of it, notice where the words flow and where they catch.
Theravada. The Buddhist tradition whose monks still ask one another's forgiveness, and whose practice gives this chant its roots. Today's word.
Your line: I ask, I forgive. Out, in, and back, as often as it takes. That's day nine hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: In Theravada communities, monks and lay people ask one another's forgiveness in set words at certain times, and meditation teachers teach a forgiveness practice that asks, gives and turns forgiveness toward oneself, repeated slowly over time.

chat.says: Why does that forgiveness practice say 'knowingly or unknowingly'?
options: Some harm we did we'll never know about, and some done to us wasn't meant.
Only harm done on purpose counts, so it helps sort out the real wrongs.
It means you only forgive people who didn't know what they were doing.
chat.meaning: The phrase forgives without waiting for a full account: some harm we did is unknown to us, and some done to us wasn't meant.

notes: The practice lines are a paraphrase of the traditional forgiveness reflection as taught in Theravada and Western insight circles; they are described, not invented, and offered as optional ('if you'd like'). A Keeper should confirm the wording is recognizable and not read as a new prayer.
'Monks in the Theravada tradition still ask one another's forgiveness, in set words, at certain times' (e.g. khamatha me bhante, at the end of the rains or before uposatha): confirm phrasing.
DN 2 paraphrased: the Buddha's words to King Ajatasattu after his confession of killing his father. Rhys Davids 1899 is public domain but the writer isn't certain of the exact wording. Confirm.
Jack Kornfield named and paraphrased (not quoted) as a teacher of the repeated practice; confirm the attribution is fair.
No original-language word given (khamā/khamati uncertain as a game item); original is null.
Editor pass: 'over days and weeks' for Kornfield's teaching softened to 'many times, over time' (the span was unsourced).

Audit: the hook's 'a practice found in Theravada communities' overstated it: the English 'if I have harmed anyone' wording is a modern insight-meditation form (cf. Kornfield); traditional Theravada asking of forgiveness uses Pali formulas (e.g. Okasa / khamatha me bhante). Now 'with roots in Theravada practice'.
